claim: EXOSC1 promotes DNA damages in human kidney renal clear cell carcinoma (KIRC) cells.
source: Here, we show that exosome component 1 (EXOSC1) promotes DNA damages and sensitizes human kidney renal clear cell carcinoma (KIRC) cells to DNA repair inhibitor.
evidence: The abstract directly states this finding, which is supported by experimental data shown in figures including γ-H2AX staining and comet assays.

claim: EXOSC1 sensitizes human kidney renal clear cell carcinoma (KIRC) cells to DNA repair inhibitor.
source: Here, we show that exosome component 1 (EXOSC1) promotes DNA damages and sensitizes human kidney renal clear cell carcinoma (KIRC) cells to DNA repair inhibitor.
evidence: The abstract states this finding, supported by colony formation assays and xenograft experiments with PARP inhibitors.

claim: EXOSC1 preferentially cleaves C site(s) in single-stranded DNA.
source: Among the candidates, EXOSC1 most notably promoted DNA damages and subsequent mutations via preferentially cleaving C site(s) in single-stranded DNA.
evidence: The abstract states this finding, which is supported by in vitro cleavage assays and mass spectrometry analyses shown in the results.

claim: EXOSC1 was more significantly correlated with C>A transversions in coding strands than these in template strands in human KIRC.
source: Consistently, EXOSC1 was more significantly correlated with C>A transversions in coding strands than these in template strands in human KIRC.
evidence: The abstract states this finding, which is supported by statistical analyses of TCGA data comparing C>A and G>T mutations.

claim: KIRC patients with high EXOSC1 showed a poor prognosis.
source: Notably, KIRC patients with high EXOSC1 showed a poor prognosis, and EXOSC1 sensitized human cancer cells to poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase inhibitors.
evidence: The abstract states this finding, which is supported by Kaplan-Meier survival analyses of TCGA patient data.

claim: EXOSC1 sensitized human cancer cells to poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase inhibitors.
source: Notably, KIRC patients with high EXOSC1 showed a poor prognosis, and EXOSC1 sensitized human cancer cells to poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase inhibitors.
evidence: The abstract states this finding, which is supported by colony formation assays and xenograft experiments.

claim: EXOSC1 acts as an ESM in KIRC.
source: These results show that EXOSC1 acts as an ESM in KIRC, and targeting EXOSC1 might be a potential therapeutic strategy.
evidence: The abstract concludes this based on multiple lines of evidence including mutation analyses, DNA cleavage assays, and correlation with patient outcomes.

claim: Targeting EXOSC1 might be a potential therapeutic strategy.
source: These results show that EXOSC1 acts as an ESM in KIRC, and targeting EXOSC1 might be a potential therapeutic strategy.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the findings that EXOSC1 promotes mutations and sensitizes cells to PARP inhibitors.

claim: DNA damages and subsequent mutations are central to development, progression, and treatment of nearly all cancers.
source: DNA damages and subsequent mutations are central to development, progression, and treatment of nearly all cancers (Brown et al., 2017; Farmer et al., 2005; Jeggo et al., 2016; Pearl et al., 2015; Roos et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Cancer cells frequently decrease DNA repair pathways and increase endogenous sources of mutation (ESM) to drive mutations.
source: Cancer cells frequently decrease DNA repair pathways and increase endogenous sources of mutation (ESM) to drive mutations (Brown et al., 2017; Farmer et al., 2005; Jeggo et al., 2016; Pearl et al., 2015; Roos et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Cancer cells are often more reliant on a subset of DNA repair pathway(s) to survive DNA damages.
source: Hence, cancer cells are often more reliant on a subset of DNA repair pathway(s) to survive DNA damages.
evidence: This is an inference based on the previous statement about cancer cells decreasing DNA repair pathways.

claim: Targeting critical DNA repair members, such as poly (ADP-ribose) polymerases (PARPs), offers a therapeutic strategy for cancers.
source: Targeting critical DNA repair members, such as poly (ADP-ribose) polymerases (PARPs) (Brown et al., 2017; Tubbs and Nussenzweig, 2017), offers a therapeutic strategy for cancers (Tutt et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Inhibition of PARPs by small-molecule compounds disrupts the ability of cancer cells to survive ongoing DNA damage and results in cell cycle arrest and/or cell death.
source: Inhibition of PARPs by small-molecule compounds disrupts the ability of cancer cells to survive ongoing DNA damage and results in cell cycle arrest and/or cell death (Lord and Ashworth, 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The failure of PARP inhibitors (PARPis) to markedly benefit patients suggests the necessity for developing new strategies.
source: However, the failure of PARP inhibitors (PARPis) to markedly benefit patients suggests the necessity for developing new strategies.
evidence: This is an inference based on clinical observations and the need for improved therapies.

claim: ESM constantly assaults genomic DNA and almost inevitably leads to mutations.
source: ESM constantly assaults genomic DNA and almost inevitably leads to mutations (Figure 1A; Jeggo et al., 2016; Roos et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Most of the ESM studies were focused on deamination.
source: However, most of the ESM studies were focused on deamination.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the field based on the authors' review of literature.

claim: Transitions show higher frequency than expected by chance, although there are twice as many possible transversions.
source: Transitions show higher frequency than expected by chance, although there are twice as many possible transversions.
evidence: This is a well-established observation in mutation studies, supported by general knowledge.

claim: Nucleotide substitutions consist of two types: transition and transversion.
source: Nucleotide substitutions consist of two types: transition and transversion (Alexandrov et al., 2013; Burgess, 2019; Petljak et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a basic definition in genetics supported by citations.

claim: Transition is a substitution in which one base is replaced by another of the same class (purine or pyrimidine).
source: Transition is a substitution in which one base is replaced by another of the same class (purine or pyrimidine), while transversion is a substitution in which a purine is replaced with a pyrimidine or vice versa (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a basic definition in genetics illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: Transversion is a substitution in which a purine is replaced with a pyrimidine or vice versa.
source: Transition is a substitution in which one base is replaced by another of the same class (purine or pyrimidine), while transversion is a substitution in which a purine is replaced with a pyrimidine or vice versa (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a basic definition in genetics illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: C>T transitions at methylated cytosine in CG base pairs display a higher frequency than expected.
source: C>T transitions at methylated cytosine in CG base pairs display a higher frequency than expected (Alexandrov et al., 2013; Alexandrov et al., 2013; Burgess, 2019; Hutchinson, 2013; Petljak et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Activation-induced cytidine deaminase (AID) was identified as an ESM.
source: Therefore, activation-induced cytidine deaminase (AID) (Barlow et al., 2013; Greaves, 2018; Petersen-Mahrt et al., 2002) and apolipoprotein B mRNA editing enzyme catalytic (APOBEC) family (Alexandrov et al., 2013; Buisson et al., 2019; Hutchinson, 2013; McGranahan et al., 2017; Robertson et al., 2017) catalyzing the deamination of C were identified as ESMs.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: APOBEC family was identified as an ESM.
source: Therefore, activation-induced cytidine deaminase (AID) (Barlow et al., 2013; Greaves, 2018; Petersen-Mahrt et al., 2002) and apolipoprotein B mRNA editing enzyme catalytic (APOBEC) family (Alexandrov et al., 2013; Buisson et al., 2019; Hutchinson, 2013; McGranahan et al., 2017; Robertson et al., 2017) catalyzing the deamination of C were identified as ESMs.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Some cancers, such as kidney renal clear cell carcinoma (KIRC), show the low mutation proportion at CG base pairs and low APOBEC expression.
source: Unfortunately, some cancers, such as kidney renal clear cell carcinoma (KIRC), show the low mutation proportion at CG base pairs and low APOBEC expression (Burns et al., 2013b), raising the potential roles of unidentified ESMs.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: KIRC shows the low mutation proportion at CG base pairs, suggesting that the deamination contributes less to the mutations in KIRC.
source: KIRC shows the lowest proportion of mutations at CG in major cancer types (Burns et al., 2013b), suggesting that the deamination contributes less to the mutations in KIRC.
evidence: This is an inference based on cited data about mutation patterns in KIRC.

claim: Only low expressions of AID and APOBECs were detected in KIRC.
source: Only low expressions of AID and APOBECs were detected in KIRC (Burns et al., 2013b).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The kidney potentially suffers less from exogenous source of mutations (EOSMs).
source: The kidney potentially suffers less from exogenous source of mutations (EOSMs) (Loeb, 2011; Roberts and Gordenin, 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: RNA-seq and exomic mutation data corresponding to 532 KIRC patients and 30,254 somatic substitution mutations in the TCGA were retrieved from The cBio Cancer Genomics Portal.
source: RNA-seq and exomic mutation data corresponding to 532 KIRC patients and 30,254 somatic substitution mutations in the TCGA were retrieved from The cBio Cancer Genomics Portal (http://cbioportal.org) (Figure 1D).
evidence: This describes the data source used in the study.

claim: ESMs likely show a similar impact on the template and code DNA strands.
source: Because that ESMs likely show a similar impact on the template and code DNA strands, the 12 types of substitution were groups into six types of complementary substitution (c-substitution) to simplify the analyses (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is an assumption made by the authors to justify their analytical approach.

claim: GAPDH showed a p=0.0011 and r=0.16 correlation with C>A/G>T c-substitution.
source: For example, GAPDH showed a p=0.0011 and r=0.16 correlation with C>A/G>T c-substitution, indicating that GAPDH expression displayed a positive correlation with C>A/G>T (Figure 1E and Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is a specific statistical result from the Spearman's rank analysis.

claim: GAPDH expression displayed a positive correlation with C>A/G>T.
source: For example, GAPDH showed a p=0.0011 and r=0.16 correlation with C>A/G>T c-substitution, indicating that GAPDH expression displayed a positive correlation with C>A/G>T (Figure 1E and Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the statistical result.

claim: CRB3 was positively correlated with C>A/G>T.
source: Similarly, CRB3 was also positively correlated with C>A/G>T (Figure 1E and Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the analysis.

claim: Top-ranked 200 genes (approximately 1% of the genome-wide genes) were taken as the candidates for each c-substitution type.
source: Although the p values of multiple genes were lower than 0.05 (Figure 1F and Figure 1—source data 1), only top-ranked 200 genes (approximately 1% of the genome-wide genes) were taken as the candidates for each c-substitution type (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This describes the selection criteria used in the study.

claim: Top candidate genes showed the enrichment in 'mitochondrial gene expression' and 'organophosphate biosynthetic process'.
source: Gene Ontology (GO) enrichment analyses indicated that, generally, these top candidate genes showed the enrichment in 'mitochondrial gene expression' and 'organophosphate biosynthetic process' (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is a result from Gene Ontology enrichment analysis.

claim: ASNS with p=0.0005 and FC=1.39 indicates that ASNS was increased in the high group.
source: For example, ASNS with p=0.0005 and FC=1.39 indicates that ASNS was increased in the high group (Figure 1G and Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is a specific statistical result from Student's t-test analysis.

claim: None of the APOBEC family members were identified as candidate by correlation or Student's t-test analyses.
source: Notably, none of the APOBEC family members were identified as candidate by correlation or Student's t-test analyses, supporting that deamination contributes less to the mutations in KIRC.
evidence: This is a result from the statistical analyses performed in the study.

claim: KIRC displayed higher frequencies of C>A/G>T, A>T/T>A, and A>C/T>G mutations than the other four cancers did.
source: Although most frequently mutated substitutions in the five major cancers were C>T/G>A, KIRC displayed higher frequencies of C>A/G>T, A>T/T>A, and A>C/ >G mutations than the other four cancers did (Figure 1I and Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is a comparative analysis result across different cancer types.

claim: Most c-substitutions in KIRC patient mutations are function-related.
source: Among the KIRC patient mutations, most c-substitutions are function-related (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a result from analyzing the functional impact of mutations.

claim: The transversions in KIRC showed more capacities to result in function-related mutations than transitions (C>T/G>A and A>G/T>C) did.
source: Notably, the transversions in KIRC showed more capacities to result in function-related mutations than transitions (C>T/G>A and A>G/T>C) did (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a comparative analysis of mutation types and their functional consequences.

claim: The most frequent c-substitution type of TP53 mutations in BRCA was C>T/G>A.
source: Consistent with previous studies (Burns et al., 2013a; Kandoth et al., 2013), the most frequent c-substitution type of TP53 mutations in BRCA was C>T/G>A (Figure 1J and Figure 1—source data 1)
evidence: This is a result from mutation spectrum analysis, consistent with prior literature.

claim: The most frequent type of VHL mutations in KIRC was C>A/G>T (p=0.004, chi-squared test).
source: while the most frequent type of VHL mutations in KIRC was C>A/G>T (p=0.004, chi-squared test) (Figure 1K and Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is a statistical result from mutation spectrum analysis.

claim: Patients with VHL C>A/G>T mutations showed poor OS.
source: Further, Kaplan–Meier (KM) analysis of overall survival (OS) indicated that patients with VHL C>A/G>T mutations showed poor OS (Figure 1L).
evidence: This is a result from Kaplan-Meier survival analysis.

claim: CCNB1, EXOSC1, and RAB5IF were identified as candidate ESMs for C>A/G>T by all of the analyses.
source: Further overlap analyses demonstrated that cyclin B1 (CCNB1), exosome component 1 (EXOSC1), and RAB5 interacting factor (RAB5IF) were identified as candidate ESMs for C>A/G>T by all of the above analyses (Figure 1M).
evidence: This is a result from overlap analysis of multiple statistical approaches.

claim: AID enhanced mutation in E. coli.
source: Consistent with a previous study (Petersen-Mahrt et al., 2002), AID enhanced mutation in E. coli (Figure 2B and Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is a result from rifampicin-resistant assay, consistent with prior literature.

claim: EXOSC1 more significantly increased mutations than AID did (p=4.08 × 10−5).
source: Notably, EXOSC1 more significantly increased mutations than AID did (p=4.08 × 10−5) (Figure 2B and Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is a comparative statistical result from rifampicin-resistant assay.

claim: Among the members of exosome complex, EXOSC1 most notably enhanced mutation in E. coli (p=3.5 × 10−11).
source: Among the members of exosome complex, EXOSC1 most notably enhanced mutation in E. coli (p=3.5 × 10−11) (Figure 2C and Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is a comparative statistical result from rifampicin-resistant assay.

claim: IPTG absence notably decreased the mutation frequency (p=1.29 × 10−9), indicating that the protein of EXOSC1 promoted the mutation.
source: As shown in Figure 2E–F, IPTG absence notably decreased the mutation frequency (p=1.29 × 10−9), indicating that the protein of EXOSC1 promoted the mutation.
evidence: This is a result from rifampicin-resistant assay with and without IPTG induction.

claim: EXOSC1 expression only slightly decreased cell growth, which might be due to the increase in mutation burden.
source: As shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C, EXOSC1 expression only slightly decreased cell growth, which might be due to the increase in mutation burden (Schaaper and Dunn, 1987).
evidence: This is an observation from growth assays with a speculative explanation supported by citation.

claim: Most of mutations in control clones were C>T/G>A transitions, while EXOSC1 frequently promoted C>A/G>T transversion mutations.
source: Sequencing of rpoB gene in 25 randomly selected rifampicin-resistant clones indicated that most of mutations in control clones were C>T/G>A transitions, while EXOSC1 frequently promoted C>A/G>T transversion mutations (Figure 2G–I and Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is a result from sequencing analysis of rifampicin-resistant clones.

claim: Most of C>A/G>T transversions in EXOSC1-transformed cells were clustered at C1576 (10/36 mutations) and C1699 (6/36 mutations).
source: Moreover, most of C>A/G>T transversions in EXOSC1-transformed cells were clustered at C1576 (10/36 mutations) and C1699 (6/36 mutations), whereas C>T/G>A transitions in control cells showed a distinct distribution with major hot spots at C1565 (6/32 mutations) and C1721 (5/32 mutations) (Figure 2G and Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is a result from sequencing analysis showing mutation distribution.

claim: C>T/G>A transitions in control cells showed a distinct distribution with major hot spots at C1565 (6/32 mutations) and C1721 (5/32 mutations).
source: Moreover, most of C>A/G>T transversions in EXOSC1-transformed cells were clustered at C1576 (10/36 mutations) and C1699 (6/36 mutations), whereas C>T/G>A transitions in control cells showed a distinct distribution with major hot spots at C1565 (6/32 mutations) and C1721 (5/32 mutations) (Figure 2G and Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is a result from sequencing analysis showing mutation distribution.

claim: The mutations in control and EXOSC1-transformed cells were promoted by a distinct mechanism.
source: Hence, it was suggested that the mutations in control and EXOSC1-transformed cells were promoted by a distinct mechanism.
evidence: This is an inference based on the different mutation patterns observed.

claim: EXOSC1-transformed cells showed a shift of C>A/G>T mutations from 6% (2/32 mutations) to 69% (25/36 mutations) (p=4.03 × 10−7, chi-squared test).
source: Interestingly, EXOSC1-transformed cells also showed a shift of C>A/G>T mutations from 6% (2/32 mutations) to 69% (25/36 mutations) (p=4.03 × 10−7, chi-squared test) (Figure 2H–J).
evidence: This is a statistical result from mutation spectrum analysis.

claim: EXOSC1 notably cleaved ssDNA, while it displayed no detectable capability to cleave dsDNA or DNA-RNA hybrid.
source: Polyacrylamide TBE-urea gel analyses of the resultant mixtures indicated that EXOSC1 notably cleaved ssDNA, while it displayed no detectable capability to cleave dsDNA or DNA-RNA hybrid (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a result from in vitro cleavage assays.

claim: Unlike EXOSC1, none of EXOSC2–EXOSC9 detectably cleaved ssDNA.
source: Gel analyses of the resultant mixtures indicated that, unlike EXOSC1, none of EXOSC2–EXOSC9 detectably cleaved ssDNA (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a result from in vitro cleavage assays comparing exosome members.

claim: EXOSC6, EXOSC7, and EXOSC8 decreased EXOSC1 cleavage activity.
source: Interestingly, EXOSC6, EXOSC7, and EXOSC8 decreased EXOSC1 cleavage activity (Figure 3D)
evidence: This is a result from in vitro cleavage assays with different exosome members.

claim: EXOSC2, EXOSC3, EXOSC4, and EXOSC9 showed no detectable impact on EXOSC1 cleavage activity.
source: while EXOSC2, EXOSC3, EXOSC4, and EXOSC9 showed no detectable impact (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a result from in vitro cleavage assays with different exosome members.

claim: EXOSC1–9 (the exosome complex) displayed not detect DNA cleavage activity.
source: And EXOSC1–9 (the exosome complex) displayed not detect DNA cleavage activity (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is a result from in vitro cleavage assays with the complete exosome complex.

claim: K+ and Mg2+ enhanced the cleavage activity of EXOSC1.
source: It was found that K+ and Mg2+ enhanced the cleavage activity of EXOSC1 (Figure 3E)
evidence: This is a result from in vitro cleavage assays with different reaction components.

claim: EXOSC1 showed the highest cleavage activity at pH 7.0.
source: and EXOSC1 showed the highest cleavage activity at pH 7.0 (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is a result from in vitro cleavage assays at different pH values.

claim: The cleavage rate of EXOSC1 was approximately 4 × 10−4/min at 37°C.
source: Further analyses indicated that the cleavage rate of EXOSC1 was approximately 4 × 10−4/min at 37°C (Figure 3G and H).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from time course cleavage assays.

claim: EXOSC1 cleaved unbiased ssDNA and displayed no detectable capability to cleave dsDNA or DNA-RNA hybrid.
source: Consistent with the result of the generic DNA, EXOSC1 cleaved unbiased ssDNA and displayed no detectable capability to cleave dsDNA or DNA-RNA hybrid (Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a result from in vitro cleavage assays with unbiased DNA sequences.

claim: Only EXOSC1 displayed cleavage activity against unbiased ssDNA.
source: And only EXOSC1 displayed cleavage activity against unbiased ssDNA (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a result from in vitro cleavage assays comparing exosome members.

claim: The cleavage rate against unbiased ssDNA (approximately 1.2 × 10−3/min) was higher than that against generic ssDNA.
source: Interestingly, the cleavage rate against unbiased ssDNA (approximately 1.2 × 10−3/min) was higher than that against generic ssDNA (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B), suggesting that the DNA sequence might show some impact on the activity of EXOSC1.
evidence: This is a comparative result from time course cleavage assays.

claim: The DNA sequence might show some impact on the activity of EXOSC1.
source: Interestingly, the cleavage rate against unbiased ssDNA (approximately 1.2 × 10−3/min) was higher than that against generic ssDNA (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B), suggesting that the DNA sequence might show some impact on the activity of EXOSC1.
evidence: This is an inference based on the different cleavage rates observed.

claim: Mass spectrometry (MS) analyses demonstrated that the resultant mixtures contained more free C than the other three base types.
source: Notably, mass spectrometry (MS) analyses (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C and D) demonstrated that the resultant mixtures contained more free C than the other three base types (Figure 4E), suggesting that EXOSC1 preferred to cleave C sites in ssDNA.
evidence: This is a result from mass spectrometry analysis of cleavage products.

claim: EXOSC1 preferred to cleave C sites in ssDNA.
source: Notably, mass spectrometry (MS) analyses (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C and D) demonstrated that the resultant mixtures contained more free C than the other three base types (Figure 4E), suggesting that EXOSC1 preferred to cleave C sites in ssDNA.
evidence: This is an inference based on mass spectrometry results.

claim: EXOSC1 cleaved the ssDNA containing C>A hot spot of VHL mutation.
source: Consistently, EXOSC1 cleaved the ssDNA containing C>A hot spot of VHL mutation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is a result from in vitro cleavage assays with specific DNA sequences.

claim: EXOSC1 cleaved C sites in ssDNA and subsequently resulted in C>A mutations through 'A' rule DNA repair.
source: Since EXOSC1 was correlated with the C>A/G>T c-substitution type, it was likely that EXOSC1 cleaved C sites in ssDNA and subsequently resulted in C>A mutations through 'A' rule DNA repair.
evidence: This is a mechanistic inference based on the cleavage preference and mutation patterns.

claim: C>A transversions in the 'untranscribed' coding strand lead to C>A mutations in a gene, while C>A transversions in the 'transcribed' template strand result in G>T mutations.
source: As shown in Figure 4F, C>A transversions in the 'untranscribed' coding strand lead to C>A mutations in a gene, while C>A transversions in the 'transcribed' template strand result in G>T mutations.
evidence: This is an explanation of how strand asymmetry affects mutation outcomes.

claim: C>A substitution in rpoB gene was generated at a much higher frequency than G>T in EXOSC1-transformed E. coli cells.
source: As shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1F and G, C>A substitution in rpoB gene was generated at a much higher frequency than G>T.
evidence: This is a result from sequencing analysis of rifampicin-resistant clones.

claim: Compared with the control, EXOSC1 enhanced C>A from 0% to 69% (p=2.67 × 10−7), while EXOSC1 only enhanced G>T from 6% to 17% even without a significance (p=0.27).
source: Compared with the control, EXOSC1 enhanced C>A from 0% to 69% (p=2.67 × 10−7), while EXOSC1 only enhanced G>T from 6% to 17% even without a significance (p=0.27) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F and G, and Figure 4—figure supplement 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is a statistical result showing strand asymmetry in mutations.

claim: EXOSC1 showed the highest correlation (r) with C>A, and the correlation between EXOSC1 and G>T was even lower than that between EXOSC1 and C>A/G>T.
source: Spearman's rank analyses indicated that EXOSC1 showed the highest correlation (r) with C>A, and the correlation between EXOSC1 and G>T was even lower than that between EXOSC1 and C>A/G>T (Figure 4G, Figure 4—source data 1, Figure 4—figure supplement 1H, and Figure 4—figure supplement 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is a result from Spearman's rank correlation analysis.

claim: EXOSC1 showed more significant expression differences between the low and high C>A groups than those between the low and high G>T groups.
source: Importantly, EXOSC1 showed more significant expression differences between the low and high C>A groups than those between the low and high G>T groups (Figure 4H and Figure 4—figure supplement 1K), suggesting that EXOSC1 prefers to cleave C sites in ssDNA in vivo.
evidence: This is a result from Student's t-test analysis showing strand asymmetry.

claim: EXOSC1 prefers to cleave C sites in ssDNA in vivo.
source: Importantly, EXOSC1 showed more significant expression differences between the low and high C>A groups than those between the low and high G>T groups (Figure 4H and Figure 4—figure supplement 1K), suggesting that EXOSC1 prefers to cleave C sites in ssDNA in vivo.
evidence: This is an inference based on the strand asymmetry analysis.

claim: EXOSC1 increased the γ-H2AX foci in the cells.
source: γ-H2AX staining analyses of the resultant cells demonstrated that EXOSC1 increased the γ-H2AX foci in the cells (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is a result from γ-H2AX immunofluorescence staining.

claim: The number of γ-H2AX-positive cells was increased approximately sevenfold by EXOSC1.
source: The number of γ-H2AX-positive cells was increased approximately sevenfold by EXOSC1 (Figure 5B and Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from γ-H2AX staining analysis.

claim: Knockdown of EXOSC1 reduced the γ-H2AX foci.
source: While knockdown of EXOSC1 reduced the γ-H2AX foci (Figure 5C, Figure 5—source data 1, Figure 5—figure supplement 1B and C, and Figure 5—figure supplement 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is a result from γ-H2AX staining with EXOSC1 knockdown.

claim: Comet tail analyses indicated that EXOSC1 increased DNA damage.
source: Consistent with the results of γ-H2AX staining, comet tail analyses also indicated that EXOSC1 increased DNA damage (Figure 5D and E, and Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: This is a result from neutral comet tail assays.

claim: The enhanced expression of EXOSC1 (EXOSC1-OE) increased the lower temperature amplicons (LTAs) of VHL.
source: As shown in Figure 5F, the enhanced expression of EXOSC1 (EXOSC1-OE) increased the lower temperature amplicons (LTAs) of VHL, suggesting that EXOSC1 increased the mutations in VHL gene.
evidence: This is a result from 3D-PCR analysis.

claim: EXOSC1 increased the mutations in VHL gene.
source: As shown in Figure 5F, the enhanced expression of EXOSC1 (EXOSC1-OE) increased the lower temperature amplicons (LTAs) of VHL, suggesting that EXOSC1 increased the mutations in VHL gene.
evidence: This is an inference based on 3D-PCR results.

claim: EXOSC1-OE cells showed more C>A mutations in VHL gene.
source: Consistently, further sequencing analyses of the LTAs indicated that EXOSC1-OE cells showed more C>A mutations in VHL gene (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is a result from sequencing analysis of 3D-PCR products.

claim: Knockdown of XRCC1 impaired the capability of EXOSC1 to increase the LTAs.
source: 3D-PCR analyses of the resultant cells indicated that knockdown of XRCC1 impaired the capability of EXOSC1 to increase the LTAs (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is a result from 3D-PCR analysis with XRCC1 knockdown.

claim: Both XRCC1 knockdown (XRCC1-KD) and EXOSC1 knockdown (EXOSC1-KD) decreased the LTAs.
source: Furthermore, both XRCC1 knockdown (XRCC1-KD) and EXOSC1 knockdown (EXOSC1-KD) decreased the LTAs (Figure 5H and I).
evidence: This is a result from 3D-PCR analysis with knockdowns.

claim: EXOSC1 increased the LTAs of VHL in xenograft tumors, whereas knockdown of EXOSC1 reduced the LTAs.
source: Consistent with the ex vivo results, niraparib more notably inhibited the tumor with enhanced EXOSC1 (Figure 6G and I, and Figure 6—source data 1), indicating that EXOSC1 sensitized KIRC xenografts to the inhibitor.
evidence: This is a result from 3D-PCR analysis of xenograft tumors.

claim: EXOSC1 enhanced mutations in KIRC.
source: After 2 weeks, 3D-PCR analyses of the resultant tumors indicated that EXOSC1 increased the LTAs of VHL, whereas knockdown of EXOSC1 reduced the LTAs (Figure 5K), suggesting that EXOSC1 enhanced mutations in KIRC.
evidence: This is an inference based on 3D-PCR results from xenograft tumors.

claim: High EXOSC1 group showed poor DFS and OS.
